source.title: Comparative Study of Large Language Model Architectures on Frontier
source.authors: Junqi Yin; A. Bose; Guo-Jing Cong; I. Lyngaas; Quentin Anthony

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. Some plotted loss values are not given numerically in the text.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares pretraining losses across two model sizes and architecture variants, but does not fit or reproduce scaling-law curves.
record.gate_note: The paper reports loss comparisons relevant to model size and architecture, plus a comparison of loss with zero-shot benchmark performance. It also reports optimizer and tokenizer/vocabulary loss comparisons, which do not test a listed version as written. Training-throughput results and cited scaling-law findings are not rows.
record.test_reason: In a new setting (a 15B-token materials-science corpus), the study compares pretraining loss across two sizes and two architectures, and compares loss with downstream accuracy. These bear weakly on V1, V4 and V6. It fits no scaling curves and was not designed to test scaling laws.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors also conclude that NeoX and LLaMA perform similarly on generic downstream tasks, and that data quality and a larger vocabulary matter more. Loss is called an indicator of performance that does not fully correlate with downstream results.
record.recipe_differences: The study pretrains domain-specific MatGPT models at two sizes and compares their losses; it does not fit power laws across model, token and compute sweeps or search for compute-optimal allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported loss comparisons vary with optimizer and batch size, architecture, tokenizer and vocabulary. The authors caution that tokenizer/vocabulary changes alter the effective tokens and make absolute losses incomparable.

fits_no_version.finding: LAMB with a 4M batch gives about 2% lower loss than Adam with a 1M batch at 1.7B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Pretraining loss at fixed size and data depends on the optimizer/batch recipe.

fits_no_version.finding: Loss values for different tokenizers or vocabularies differ markedly but are not comparable, because effective tokens differ.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Cross-entropy loss is not comparable across tokenizations.

fits_no_version.finding: Loss curves for 1.7B trained in float16 and bfloat16 are almost identical.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training precision has a negligible effect on loss.

record.peer_reviewed: IEEE International Parallel and Distributed Processing Symposium
record.problems: Only two parameter sizes are compared for the loss-versus-size result, and no power-law fit or exponent is reported. Loss comparisons are largely qualitative in the text, with plotted values not transcribed numerically. The optimizer comparison also changes batch size, and loss comparisons across tokenizer/vocabulary variants involve different effective tokens.
record.rows_left_out: No separately stated loss or downstream comparisons bearing on the tested versions were left out. Exact values visible only in plots are not recoverable from the supplied text.

untested.parts: Power-law form, token and compute scaling, several orders of magnitude; only two model sizes are compared.
Depth/width variation at fixed parameter count. The Fig. 4 shape grid reports throughput only, not loss.
Any fitted relation of downstream accuracy to scale or loss; no across-size downstream comparison is stated in text.
Not tested; Chinchilla is only cited to choose model size.

missing.what: Few-shot (3- and 5-shot) comparison at 6.7B: LLaMA better on 3/9 tasks, NeoX on 3/9. Bears on whether loss tracks downstream accuracy.

Band-gap MAE with LLM embeddings. The best result is MatGPT-NeoX 6.7B (+GPT 0.197 vs +SciBERT 0.204). The authors say larger models and hidden sizes perform better; downstream accuracy improves with scale.
missing.locator: Sec. IV-B, Fine-tuning for Scientific Task; Table V

record.verdict_notes: This is an HPC and architecture comparison study whose scaling evidence is incidental. V4 is tested via normalization/activation differences, not depth/width. The recipe used for the size comparison and for the zero-shot checkpoints is not stated explicitly. The Fig. 4 layer/hidden-size grid measures throughput, not loss, so it is not V4 evidence.

versions.untested_parts: Tests loss against parameter count for MatGPT-LLaMA at 1.7B and 6.7B with the same HF tokenizer and 52K vocabulary. Does not test token-count or compute scaling, several orders of magnitude, or a fitted power law.
No small-run fit or prediction of larger-run loss.
No fixed-compute search for a loss-minimising parameter/token allocation.
Compares GPT-NeoX and LLaMA loss at matched model sizes and reported training recipes. Does not systematically vary depth and width at fixed parameter count to test a wide range of architectures.
No other modality, repeated-data, fine-tuning or transfer scaling-law test.
Compares zero-shot benchmark outcomes with loss-related model comparisons, but does not fit a predictive relationship between downstream performance and pretraining loss or scale.
Does not estimate scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocations, compare fitting methods, or test whether curves bend away from a power law.
